core_relation.sentence: The scholarly credibility of the bodily resurrection view depends on critical scholars themselves affirming that Paul and the disciples saw the same bodily Jesus described in the Gospels.
core_relation.quote: He teaches the same bodily appearances Matthew, Luke, and John do. [S024]

product_test.quote: You have got to make this distinguish between what Paul said and somebody else going "Well, Bultmann says Paul believed bodily resurrection." No, he didn't. [S032][S033]
product_test.reason: The argument collapses if the critical scholar's own testimony is removed: the point is not merely that resurrection is probable, but that even hostile or non-committal scholars concede the bodily appearance. If the scholar does not concede it, the specific evidentiary force Habermas is citing is zero, not merely weakened.

slots.plays_role: External negentropy influx: the published German scholarly volumes and the broader critical academy supply credibility from outside Habermas's own theological camp.
slots.quote: Now, see, the Germans have already published these things, so you know there's a certain credibility of scholarship. German scholarship still means German scholarship. [S018][S019]

slots.plays_role: Alignment: the force of the testimony depends on the scholar being aligned with the critical reference frame, not with conservative Christianity.
slots.quote: But, you wouldn't blame him with being one of these fighting fundy type guys at all. [S038]

slots.plays_role: Signal fidelity: the exact wording of the scholars' statements is carefully preserved and repeated so that the claim survives transmission.
slots.quote: I believe that the disciples saw Jesus and that he saw them and next Easter will find me in church. [S074]

slots.plays_role: Effective entropy: the confusion between what Paul said and what Bultmann or others say Paul said lowers the clarity of the evidence.
slots.quote: You have got to make this distinguish between what Paul said and somebody else going "Well, Bultmann says Paul believed bodily resurrection." No, he didn't. [S032][S033]

slots.plays_role: Temporal integration: the argument accumulates force over decades of scholarship, from early unpopularity to widespread acceptance.
slots.quote: That's extremely impo- unpopular when this these books first came out or even after. But now it's kind of taken the day, the fact that Paul believes in bodily resurrection is very widely taught today. [S026][S027]

slots.plays_role: Compression: the whole case is compressed into memorable one-sentence quotes from key scholars.
slots.quote: It's only It's only a sentence. It's very, very brief. [S064][S065]

slots.plays_role: Phase transition: a scholar changing their view or a consensus shifting from unpopular to widely taught marks a threshold change, not just a degree change.
slots.quote: Or when someone actually changes their view. And you know where they are. [S054][S055]

slots.plays_role: Superposition: Dale Allison holds open non-bodily possibilities while still affirming Paul meant bodily resurrection.
slots.quote: Dale says, "I'm more open to non-bodily things but I am telling you even though I'm not on that interpret- I'm not in the bodily side in my view, I think Paul meant bodily resurrection." [S031]

slots.plays_role: Non-local correlation: the testimony of one scholar is linked to others—Cook, Wright, Licona, Gundry, Allison—forming a correlated body of witnesses.
slots.quote: Uh Tom Wright has some comments just like that. So, does Michael Licona. So, does um uh Gundry in his book on Soma. [S040][S041][S042]

slots.plays_role: Integration: Habermas himself is the local integrator who collects, orders, and presents these scattered scholarly statements.
slots.quote: Anyway, I I could sit here all day and give you a hundred of those. It take me time to get them here and order them, but that one by Dale probably takes the cake. [S083][S084]

one_line: The paper's argument is an analog of the master equation in which critical scholars' own bodily-resurrection testimony multiplies into a cumulative case, but the analogy is strained by the absence of a clear external negentropy source and by social factors outside the ten slots.
breaks: The analogy treats the scholars' statements as independent evidence, but the paper explicitly notes that some scholars are friends or co-authors (Ben and John Cook), so the non-local correlation may be partly social rather than evidential.
The slot S_eff is stretched: entropy in the master equation is a physical quantity, while here it is confusion or misattribution in scholarly discourse.
The paper does not treat G as a necessary external source of coherence; German scholarship is cited as a credibility marker, not as an ongoing negentropy influx.
extra_factors: Personal relationship and friendship with scholars (Ben knows John Cook) functions as an extra factor not captured by the ten slots.
The emotional or aesthetic force of a quote ('takes the cake', 'pretty cool') adds a rhetorical factor beyond the product model.
